questions.q: What problem did physicists call the 'particle zoo' in the early 1960s?
options: Atoms had been shown to contain only three particles, which seemed too few to explain chemistry
Accelerators had revealed more than a hundred so-called fundamental particles, far too many to all be truly elementary
Particles kept escaping from the detectors before they could be measured
Every new particle turned out to be a different form of the photon
questions.explanation: By the early 1960s accelerators had produced over a hundred supposedly fundamental particles, with hundreds more fleeting resonances. The whole point of a fundamental particle is that there should be only a few, so a hundred of them was 'the absence of an answer' — physicists nicknamed the mess the particle zoo.

questions.q: What was the significance of Gell-Mann's predicted omega-minus particle?
options: It proved that quarks could be knocked free from protons
It was a naked prediction from the Eightfold Way pattern — an unseen particle with specific charge, strangeness and mass — that was then found at Brookhaven, confirming the pattern was real
It was the first particle ever shown to carry fractional charge
It was the fourth quark, charm, discovered in the November Revolution
questions.explanation: The Eightfold Way's baryon decuplet had one empty corner. Gell-Mann read off the missing particle's charge (−1), strangeness (−3) and mass directly from the geometry. When the omega-minus was found at Brookhaven in 1964 with exactly those properties, it confirmed the pattern was a genuine feature of nature, not just bookkeeping.

questions.q: Why were physicists so reluctant to accept that quarks were real when Gell-Mann first proposed them in 1964?
options: The mathematics of SU(3) symmetry had not yet been invented
Quarks would have to carry fractional charge, and no free quark — and so no fractional charge — was ever found despite extensive searching
Gell-Mann admitted he had made an arithmetic error in the proton's charge
Accelerators were not yet powerful enough to produce any new particles
questions.explanation: Quarks needed charges of +2/3 and −1/3, fractions never before observed. Searches in cosmic rays, seawater, moon rocks and more found no free quark or fractional charge, so most physicists treated quarks as a mere accounting trick. Even Gell-Mann hedged in his own paper.

questions.q: How did the SLAC deep inelastic scattering experiment reveal structure inside the proton?
options: The electrons all passed straight through, showing the proton was empty space
Hard, large-angle scatters occurred far more often than expected for a soft diffuse blob, showing there were small, hard, point-like objects inside — echoing Rutherford's gold-foil result
The protons emitted free quarks that were caught in the spectrometers
The electrons were absorbed, proving the proton was a smooth ball of charge
questions.explanation: A soft, smeared-out charge can only deflect a probe gently, so deep large-angle scattering should have been rare. Instead Friedman, Kendall and Taylor saw violent large-angle scatters again and again — the same signature Rutherford used to infer the nucleus. The proton was 'a bag of marbles', containing small hard point-like constituents.

questions.q: What is colour confinement, the reason a single quark can never be seen alone?
options: Quarks are too small for any detector to resolve individually

A single quark carries one unit of colour charge and is never colour-neutral, and the strong force grows with distance, so pulling quarks apart creates new quark-antiquark pairs rather than freeing one
Quarks decay into photons the instant they leave a proton
The electromagnetic force binds quarks too tightly to separate
questions.explanation: Only colour-neutral ('white') combinations are allowed to exist freely. A lone quark always carries one colour, so it can never be neutral. As you pull quarks apart the strong force stays constant or grows, storing energy in a flux tube that snaps into a new quark-antiquark pair — you make more particles instead of freeing a quark.

questions.q: In the quark model, what is a baryon and what holds it together?
options: A quark paired with an antiquark, a colour and its anticolour, held by electromagnetism
Three quarks bound by the strong force in a colour-neutral (red-green-blue → white) combination, such as a proton or neutron
A single quark carrying a fractional charge, held by gravity
A particle made entirely of gluons with no quarks inside
questions.explanation: A baryon is three quarks held together by the strong force, with one red, one green and one blue colour charge cancelling to white. Protons (uud) and neutrons (udd) are baryons. A quark-antiquark pair is instead a meson, like the pion.

questions.q: What is asymptotic freedom, and why did it explain Feynman's 'free' partons?
options: The strong force vanishes entirely once quarks are inside a proton, so quarks never interact
The strong force becomes very weak when quarks are very close together at high energy, so in the violent SLAC collisions the partons rattled around almost freely
Quarks gain mass as they slow down, freezing them in place
Gluons repel one another, pushing quarks apart at short range
questions.explanation: Asymptotic freedom, proven in 1973 by Gross, Wilczek and Politzer, means the strong force weakens at short distances and high energies. That is why the partons inside the proton looked like free particles in the high-energy SLAC scatters, even though the same force traps them forever at larger distances.

questions.q: From memory: explain how the SLAC deep inelastic scattering experiment is the modern parallel of Rutherford's gold-foil experiment.
keyPoints: Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil; most passed through but a few bounced back at wild angles, revealing a small hard dense nucleus inside the atom.
SLAC fired high-energy electrons at protons (liquid hydrogen); unexpectedly frequent hard large-angle scatters revealed small, hard, point-like constituents inside the proton.
In both cases you learn what is inside something by firing a probe at it and reading the scattering pattern as a map of the internal structure.
The point-like constituents in the proton turned out to be quarks, just as Rutherford's centre turned out to be the nucleus.
questions.explanation: If you connected 'fire a probe, watch the scattering, infer hard internal structure' across both experiments and named quarks as the SLAC analogue of the nucleus, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: why does pulling two quarks apart never free a single quark? Describe what happens to the string of strong-force field between them.
keyPoints: The strong force does not weaken with distance; the field forms a tense flux tube (string) between the quarks whose stored energy grows as you stretch it.
When the string holds enough energy it snaps, and that energy converts into matter via E = mc², creating a new quark-antiquark pair at the break point.
Instead of two free quarks you end up with two new colour-neutral particles, each still hiding its quark — like cutting a magnet and getting two complete magnets.
So no isolated quark is ever produced, no matter how hard you pull. This is confinement, a law of nature, not a limit of our machines.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that the energy you put into stretching becomes new particles (E = mc²) rather than a freed quark. If you recalled the snapping string and pair creation, mark it Good or Easy.

questions.q: Show that the quark content of the proton (two up quarks and one down quark) gives the correct total charge of +1, using up = +2/3 and down = −1/3 in units of the elementary charge.
questions.given: Proton = u u d,  with charges \(q_u = +\tfrac{2}{3}\),  \(q_d = -\tfrac{1}{3}\)
questions.explanation: The fractional charges, impossible as they seemed, conspire to give exactly the whole-number charge we observe. For the neutron (udd): 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0, again exactly right.

questions.q: Why did probing inside the proton require electrons of enormous energy, such as the 20 GeV beam at SLAC?
options: High energy was needed to heat the proton until it released its quarks

A moving particle behaves like a wave (de Broglie, \(\lambda = h/p\)); higher energy means shorter wavelength, and to resolve something as tiny as a proton you need a wavelength smaller than the proton
Only very fast electrons can carry a fractional charge
High energy slows the electrons down so they spend longer inside the proton
questions.explanation: Every moving particle has a de Broglie wavelength \(\lambda = h/p\) that shrinks as energy (momentum) rises. To resolve structure inside a proton (about one femtometre across) you need a wavelength smaller than the proton, which demands the staggeringly energetic electrons that only a two-mile accelerator like SLAC could produce.
